cards.a: Policing enforces a rate by dropping (or re-marking) excess traffic; it does not buffer. It uses the token bucket model and works on ingress or egress. Policing is burst-sensitive, adds no delay, and is often used to meter customer or class rates.

cards.q: How do policing and shaping differ in how they handle excess traffic, delay, and location?
cards.a: Policing drops/re-marks excess with no added delay and works on ingress or egress; shaping buffers excess, adds delay, and works egress-only. Policing drops; shaping delays.

cards.q: What do CIR, Bc, and Be mean in the token bucket model?
cards.a: CIR is the fill rate (bps), Bc is the committed burst, and Be is the excess burst. Packets that conform (tokens available) pass; those that exceed (no tokens) get dropped or re-marked.

cards.q: What are the three policing actions and when is each used?
cards.a: transmit (when traffic conforms), drop (when it violates), and set dscp plus transmit (to re-mark traffic that exceeds). Re-mark and transmit is gentler than dropping.

cards.q: What command configures a policer and its actions?
cards.a: police cir <rate> bc <burst> be <burst>, followed by conform-action, exceed-action, and violate-action. It is configured inside a policy-map class that is attached with service-policy.

cards.q: In the dual-bucket policing model, what are the three states and their actions?
cards.a: conform (Bc available) = transmit; exceed (only Be available) = re-mark; violate (no tokens) = drop. The dual-bucket model gives three outcomes.

cards.q: What command attaches a policer to the ingress of an interface?
cards.a: service-policy input <policy-map-name> under the interface. Output uses service-policy output instead.

cards.q: Where is policing commonly used and why?
cards.a: Customer rate limiting (enforce SLAs), bandwidth control (meter classes), mark-down (re-mark over rate), and ingress protection (stop floods).

cards.q: What command shows whether policing is being applied and matching rates?
cards.a: show policy-map interface (or show policy-map interface Gi0/1) shows per-interface policing stats.

cards.q: Traffic is being dropped too aggressively by a policer; what is the likely cause and fix?
cards.a: The burst size (Bc/Be) is too small. Increase bc/be so legitimate bursts conform.

cards.q: How does policing differ from shaping in terms of buffering?
cards.a: Policing never buffers; it drops or re-marks excess traffic, whereas shaping buffers the excess.

cards.q: Can policing be applied on egress?
cards.a: Yes, policing works on ingress or egress, whereas shaping is egress-only.

cards.q: Re-marking is not working on a policer even though traffic exceeds the rate; what should you check?
cards.a: Check the conform-action/exceed-action (and violate-action) statements in the police command configuration.
